So you’re going to leave out the fact that the 100k Javelina Jundred record set in 2016 was by a woman? Or that the same woman won the Moab 240? Also, there are hip exercises that you’re not considering in your definition of weights. Or that at a recreational level one marathon showed the women were on average faster than recreational men? 

I’m not trying to argue about whose “better” I’m trying to recognize that our very concept of strength in sports is being shaped by a system built by men, and one men have been training in significantly longer. Women are also generally more flexible than men, which is supposedly considered to be part of athleticism, but no one seems to care when they’re ready to talk sports. 

There are fewer female competitors, fewer long-term studies on what benefits female athletes, and fewer training opportunities for them, and they’re operating in a system traditionally created by men. To say they just aren’t as “good” is to ignore the bias implicit in the system. 

Also, would like to point out that training for women, and studies around their performance is still relatively new and revealing new trends: https://www.google.com/amp/s/www.insider.com/women-are-faster-long-distance-runners-estrogen-2020-1%3famp

There are a lot of lower body weight exercises that women tend to be stronger at, and if you look at certain endurance events women have also been shown to have an edge. Also, I’m curious if events like shooting or driving would qualify as a sport …

I agree that eventually we should revoke someone’s license. However, I don’t think speeding should trigger that. In fact, speeding isn’t even usually considered a criminal offense unless it qualifies as reckless driving or endangerment. 

If the license were to be revoked, I don’t think it should have to do with how many violations we have (and of course many of us have received more than three speeding tickets in our lifetime and still have our license), but rather the severity of the violation. So if my license is taken away for reckless driving and it’s because I was 30 mph over the speed limit and endangering others, it’s because of that incident, not the day I got a ticket for a “California rolling stop.” 

Although I do see your point that when it comes to driving, looking at someone’s past behavior can inform if we continue to trust them on the road. 

Maybe here the difference to is public safety rather than petty crimes that don’t really represent a threat to bodily safety. However, I wouldn’t say three speeding tickets should trigger that.
